label: Mark van Roojen, Moral Cognitivism vs §2.1…: Moral sentences, even with the most general moral…
locator: §2.1, 'Some theorists who view themselves as emotivists suggest that even the most general terms of moral evaluation have a descriptive meaning rather than just an emotive or non-cognitive meaning (Stevenson 1944, 22'
interpretation: Stevenson's emotivism as the entry reports it: moral terms have emotive meaning (they express and perhaps evoke emotion, §2.1) and also a descriptive meaning. Read as: every moral sentence has some descriptive meaning; what it is is not formalized. Part of the Stevenson theory bundle (#185). Attribution reading on a secondary witness: the claim records the position the entry reports, not a thesis of the entry's author. This remains a secondary-witness reading of the cited 1944 account. The separately pinned 1937 article supplies the distinct reading STEVENSON-1937-27-29-INTEREST-DISAGREEMENT; it does not retroactively replace this claim’s witness.
